introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2019. Time allowed: two and a half hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One hour, "Answer all Questions"): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, *[4 marks]*

(ii) With the aid of diagrams explain the band theory. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.**

| | Intrinsic semiconductor | Extrinsic semiconductor |
|---|---|---|
| Composition | A **pure** semiconductor (e.g. pure silicon or germanium), with no added impurities | A pure semiconductor **doped** with a small amount of an impurity (a group V donor such as phosphorus, or a group III acceptor such as boron) |
| Charge carriers | Electrons and holes in **equal numbers**, produced only by thermal excitation | Mainly one kind: **electrons** (n-type) or **holes** (p-type), the majority carriers, in addition to the thermally produced ones |
| Conductivity | Low, and strongly dependent on temperature | Much **higher**, controlled by the doping level, so it can be designed |

**(ii) Band theory.** In an isolated atom the electrons have discrete energy levels. In a solid, the interaction between the very many atoms, together with the Pauli exclusion principle, spreads each level into a closely spaced **energy band**. The highest band that is occupied by electrons at $0\ \mathrm{K}$ is the **valence band**; above it lies the **conduction band**; between them there is a **forbidden gap** (band gap) $E_g$ of energies that electrons cannot have. Only electrons in a partly filled band (the conduction band) can move freely and conduct.

**Diagrams (to be drawn by the candidate):** three energy-level diagrams, with energy on the vertical axis and the bands drawn as shaded rectangles.

- **Metal (conductor):** the valence and conduction bands **overlap**, or the band is only partly filled, so there are always free electrons.
- **Insulator:** the valence band is full, the conduction band is empty and the gap is **large** (about $5\ \mathrm{eV}$ or more): electrons cannot cross it at normal temperatures.
- **Semiconductor:** the gap is **small** ($1.1\ \mathrm{eV}$ for silicon, $0.7\ \mathrm{eV}$ for germanium). At room temperature some electrons gain enough thermal energy to jump to the conduction band, leaving **holes** in the valence band; both carry current. In doped semiconductors, donor levels lie just below the conduction band (n-type) and acceptor levels just above the valence band (p-type).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Figure 3 shows a simple amplifier circuit.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2019-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_10_fig_1.png)

When the Collector-emitter Voltage is between $+1\ \mathrm{V}$ and $+9\ \mathrm{V}$, the Collector Current is $60\,I_B$, the base-emitter voltage is $0.7\ \mathrm{V}$.

(i) Identify the type of amplifier

(ii) Calculate the base current;

(iii) the output voltage; and

(iv) the voltage gain. *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reading the circuit.** An npn transistor with its **emitter connected to the $0\ \mathrm{V}$ line**, which is common to the input $V_i$ and to the output $V_o$. The $9\ \mathrm{V}$ supply feeds the base through the $400\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor and the collector through the $1.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ load resistor; the capacitor $C$ couples the collector to the output $V_o$.

**(i) Type of amplifier.** A **common-emitter (npn) voltage amplifier**: the emitter is common to the input and output circuits, and the output is taken from the collector. It is an **inverting** amplifier.

**(ii) Base current.** The base is fed from the $9\ \mathrm{V}$ line through the $400\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor, and the base-emitter p.d. is $0.7\ \mathrm{V}$:
$$I_B = \frac{9 - 0.7}{400\times10^{3}} = \frac{8.3}{4.00\times10^{5}} = 2.08\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{A} = 20.8\ \mu\mathrm{A}$$

**(iii) Output voltage.** Collector current: $I_C = 60I_B = 60\times2.075\times10^{-5} = 1.245\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A} = 1.25\ \mathrm{mA}$.

The output voltage is the collector voltage:
$$V_o = 9 - I_CR_C = 9 - 1.245\times10^{-3}\times1.0\times10^{3} = 9 - 1.245 = 7.76\ \mathrm{V}$$
This lies between $+1\ \mathrm{V}$ and $+9\ \mathrm{V}$, so the stated condition ($I_C = 60I_B$) is satisfied.

**(iv) Voltage gain.** The input voltage is the base-emitter voltage $0.7\ \mathrm{V}$:
$$\text{voltage gain} = \frac{V_o}{V_i} = \frac{7.76}{0.7} = 11.1\ (\approx 11)$$

**Answers: common-emitter amplifier; $I_B \approx 20.8\ \mu\mathrm{A}$; $V_o \approx 7.76\ \mathrm{V}$; voltage gain $\approx 11$.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Compare the functions of a diode and a capacitor in an electric circuit *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| | Diode | Capacitor |
|---|---|---|
| Main function | Allows current in **one direction only** (low resistance when forward biased, very high when reverse biased): used for **rectification** (a.c. to d.c.) and as a detector | **Stores charge** (electrical energy) and **blocks direct current while passing alternating current**: used for smoothing, filtering, coupling stages and timing |
| Behaviour | Conducts only above a threshold forward p.d. ($\approx0.6\ \mathrm{V}$ for silicon) | Charges and discharges through a resistor (time constant $RC$) |

For example, in a power supply the diode **rectifies**, and the capacitor then **smooths** the rectified output.
